sum: Airbnb, the popular peer-to-peer home rental platform, has seen its stock surge in after-hours trading, buoyed by a robust performance in the third quarter and optimistic forecasts for the remainder of the year. The company’s CEO, Brian Chesky, celebrated the results, stating, “Airbnb is back in growth mode.” He highlighted the rarity of a marketplace of Airbnb’s magnitude reaccelerating growth, emphasizing the significant momentum the company is experiencing.

In its latest earnings report, Airbnb revealed earnings per share of $3.16, comfortably exceeding Wall Street’s estimated figures of $2.85 per share, as per S&P Global Market Intelligence data. The company’s revenue for the quarter reached $4.87 billion, representing a 19% increase and surpassing analyst expectations of $4.74 billion.

Airbnb reported particularly strong booking figures in North America, noting that nights booked had grown at their fastest pace in four years. The company also acknowledged a notable trend: not only are previous guests returning to the platform, but there is an increase in first-time users discovering the service.

The encouraging results prompted Airbnb to revise its guidance for the fourth quarter, predicting revenue growth of 16% to 19%, which translates to an estimated range of $3.22 billion to $3.28 billion. This forecast also exceeds the midpoint estimate of $3.16 billion projected by analysts. For the full fiscal year, Airbnb anticipates revenue growth in the high teens, alongside an expectation that adjusted EBITDA margins will rise to approximately 36%.

This strong performance underscores the resilience of Airbnb in the face of global travel demand, indicating a positive trajectory as the company continues to capitalize on market trends and consumer preferences.

The market expects Airbnb's third-quarter revenue to be approximately $4.75 billion, with earnings per share of around $2.85 to $2.89. The company previously guided for revenue between $4.69 billion and $4.77 billion; therefore, whether actual revenue can exceed the top end of the guidance range and whether fourth-quarter booking trends remain stable will be the core factors determining the stock's direction.

The quarter's performance largely depends on whether global travel spending continues to remain active. Airbnb expects third-quarter nights and experiences booked to achieve low double-digit growth, with average daily rates also expected to rise moderately. If bookings and daily rates improve in tandem, the platform's gross booking value will be supported, further translating into revenue growth. Demand trends across North America, Europe, Latin America, and the Asia-Pacific region are particularly worth watching, while user growth in expansion markets such as India and Brazil could also provide new booking sources for the platform.

Unlike traditional hotel operators, Airbnb primarily relies on its platform to connect hosts with travelers, and its business expansion does not entirely depend on capital investments in owned properties. As the platform's reach expands, a mutually reinforcing relationship can develop among listing supply, user activity, and booking conversion rates.

sum: Airbnb will report its third-quarter results after the market close on Thursday, November 5. The earnings preview from StockStory puts revenue growth, booking volumes and the company's ability to sustain momentum at the center of investor attention.

Airbnb generated revenue of 3.61 billion US dollars in the second quarter, an increase of 16.5 percent from a year earlier, according to the preview. The company also reported 148 million nights booked, up 10.4 percent year over year, while beating analysts' revenue expectations in that quarter.

For the third quarter, the market expects Airbnb's revenue to grow 15.9 percent year over year, StockStory said. That would represent an improvement from the 9.7 percent increase recorded in the same quarter last year. Analysts have broadly maintained their estimates over the past 30 days, pointing to expectations for continued execution rather than a major change in the operating outlook.

The key question for investors is whether booking growth remains the main driver of the business or whether the reported expansion depends more heavily on pricing and mix. The previous quarter's increase in nights booked provides a demanding reference point for the upcoming release. Airbnb's results will also show whether investment in product development and other growth initiatives is weighing on profitability as the company expands its platform.

Recent results from other consumer-internet companies provide an uneven backdrop. StockStory said Booking's revenue declined 1.3 percent year over year and missed analysts' expectations by 7 percent, while Fiverr's revenue fell 15.8 percent but exceeded expectations by 8.4 percent. These outcomes underline the importance of company-specific booking trends and guidance in Airbnb's release.

sum: A number of stocks jumped in the afternoon session after Crude oil prices plunged more than 7% on hopes of Middle East diplomatic progress, lowering the projected cost of moving people and goods. In market coverage carried by CNBC, consumer discretionary advanced 3% during morning trade as capital rotated toward cyclical groups. Financials and industrials added more than 1%. Travel, delivery, gig, and marketplace names were higher with that bid.Crude prices retreated as Brent fell 7.7% to $104.66 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate dropped 7.3% to $96.50 after Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the administration would prefer to resolve the conflict with Iran peacefully, CNBC reported. Iran’s president said the supreme leader had granted the government authority to pursue talks. Cyclical momentum was reinforced by the Institute for Supply Management, which reported its factory activity gauge rose to 55.5 in October from 54.5 in September, exceeding the 54.5 consensus from economists surveyed by Reuters.

Reuters said the pickup came with strong domestic demand.Fuel is a direct cost for a trip booked on Airbnb and for a DoorDash delivery, and it sits inside the price a household pays before it spends on a marketplace. Upwork, Fiverr, and Etsy take their volume from that same discretionary wallet. Although the survey’s prices-paid gauge registered an elevated 75.2, the pullback in benchmark crude lowers the near-term cost of travel and delivery.When energy overhead eases while domestic demand is still expanding, consumer platforms capture more orders without a higher fuel bill attached to each one. That dynamic accelerates capital rotation out of defensives and into cyclical networks whose activity rises as the cost of moving the customer falls.

sum: Is ABNB a good stock to buy? We came across a bullish thesis on Airbnb, Inc. on Astute Optics - US's Substack. In this article, we will summarize the bulls' thesis on ABNB. Airbnb, Inc.'s share was trading at $163.23 as of October 8th 2026. ABNB's trailing and forward P/E were 34.15 and 25.38 respectively according to Yahoo Finance.

This isn't the first time we see a vacation rental platform pitched as a great investment. ABNB shares gained 33.69% over the last 12 months. Comparable stocks like Expedia Group (EXPE) gained 19.39% during the same period. Why are travel stocks rising so much and is it really a good time to buy them?

In July, we published an article about the 8 Best Stocks to Buy Following Federal Reserve Pivot Expectations and ABNB ranked #4 in that article. ABNB returned 11.54% since then. So, hedge funds were right about ABNB. This article explains why hedge funds were bullish on ABNB. Airbnb, Inc. (NASDAQ:ABNB) operates a global online marketplace connecting hosts and guests for stays, experiences, and services. The big question for investors is whether Airbnb can keep growing beyond home rentals into hotels, Experiences, Services, advertising, and AI-powered travel tools, even as regulators tighten the rules around short-term rentals. Airbnb's business model requires little capital, runs on healthy margins, and its bookings are growing faster than major rivals in online travel.

Airbnb (ABNB) lost 7.56% on September 23, closing at $149.58, and no earnings miss or guidance cut caused it. The stock fell because online travel names sold off together and because Wall Street’s newest voice on the stock told investors to expect little from here. That is a strange reason to lose $12 in a day, and it is exactly why the drop is worth a closer look.

The selloff leaves ABNB about 23% below its 52-week high of $193.45, back to where it traded in late July. For a business that beat revenue estimates in each of the last five quarters and still runs a free-cash-flow margin near 37%, a market that suddenly wants to pay less deserves an answer: is this fear rational, or is it an opening?

On September 16, Morgan Stanley analyst Matthew Cost assumed coverage of the online travel sector, rating Booking Holdings Overweight, Airbnb Equal-Weight at a $170 target, and Expedia Underweight. The Airbnb call was not bearish in isolation. Cost lifted the stock from a prior Underweight stance, citing its roughly 90% direct-booking share and improved product execution as reasons double-digit room-night growth now looks more credible. But Booking was the bank’s preferred name in the group, and once the stock slid under $170, the initiation read as a ceiling rather than a floor.

In the two weeks prior, Rosenblatt and DA Davidson both started Airbnb at Buy with $220 targets, and Raymond James upgraded it to Outperform at $200. When a name known for bullish coverage picks up a high-profile neutral voice, the marginal buyer hesitates. That hesitation, layered on a broad consumer-discretionary selloff driven by rising Treasury yields, did the damage.

A second thread is also at work. Airbnb recently expanded in-app grocery ordering through a partnership with Instacart across the United States, with Canada expected to follow. Investors have not embraced it as a real revenue driver, and the muted reaction fed a broader worry that Airbnb’s services push spreads effort without moving the financial needle. That skepticism collides with what management says these extensions are for.

sum: Meta's new AI agent can book a flight or hotel room without ever visiting Expedia, Airbnb, or Booking Holdings, and Wall Street is now asking whether the aggregator business model has a future at all.

Online travel booking stocks are selling off in Wednesday morning trading as the market reprices the aggregator model against Muse, the personal artificial intelligence (AI) agent from Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META | META Price Prediction). Muse can search, compare and complete a booking directly with an airline or a hotel, removing the reason a traveler would pass through an aggregator and the fee that goes with it. Meta Platforms stock is at $751.12, up 2% as the platform whose agent is the source of the threat.

The Consumer Discretionary Select Sector SPDR Fund (NYSEARCA:XLY) is down 2% in the same session. The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is down 1%. Both are lower, yet the travel names are falling far more sharply, which marks this as a repricing of the middle layer rather than consumer weakness or a broad tech selloff.

Expedia Group (NASDAQ:EXPE) stock is at $260.33, down 7% in Wednesday morning trading. Also declining, Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB) stock is at $151.66, down 6% in the same session. Booking Holdings (NASDAQ:BKNG) stock is at $156.02, down 5% on the same thesis.

The concern for online travel booking companies is disintermediation. An agent that can execute a full booking on a traveler’s behalf turns aggregator sites into a step the customer no longer has to visit, and the commission goes with it. Expedia Group carries the heaviest loss of the three, which fits the thesis, since the business closest to pure aggregation has the least to offer a traveler whose agent can go straight to the supplier.

Goldman Sachs warned in a trading desk note that industries built on recurring bills, add-on charges and customer passivity face significant disruption from agents of this kind. The selling has spread beyond travel into financials, insurance and telecom, which is why this reads as a broader re-underwriting of middleman business models rather than a travel-demand story. Expedia, Airbnb and Booking Holdings have posted no company-specific disclosure for Wednesday’s session, so the three are falling on that shared thesis.

sum: Book lovers can temporarily ditch their day job and become the owner of a real second-hand bookshop thanks to an unusual Airbnb in Scotland.

The Open Book, located in the small town of Wigtown in Galloway, isn’t simply accommodation decorated to look like a bookstore. Guests sleep in an apartment above the shop and are handed control of the business downstairs for the duration of their visit.
That means actually opening the doors to customers and experiencing what it’s like to operate an independent bookshop.
Open Book Airbnb gives guests the keys to their own bookshop
How seriously guests take their new occupation is largely up to them. They’re allowed to rearrange displays, decide how much individual titles should cost, and even adjust the opening hours.

They can even host events inside the shop. Previous guests have organized everything from quizzes and author talks to karaoke, treasure hunts, and wine tastings, with enough room for an audience of around 12 to 15 people.
Despite temporarily becoming a bookseller, guests aren’t expected to sleep among the stock. The Airbnb includes a separate self-catering apartment directly above the shop.

Why Airbnb Stock Surged And The Rest Of Travel Did Not
sum: Its travel rivals moved a fraction as much in the same session, which points most of the explanation back inside Airbnb’s own product.

Airbnb (ABNB) stock jumped 17.4% in a single Friday session, closing at $178.07, right at the top of its 52-week range. Second-quarter results and a raised 2026 outlook were the trigger. What re-rated the stock, though, is narrower than travel demand: the company is now producing its own growth inside its own product and paying less to serve each booking.

The rest of the travel trade barely budged by comparison. BKNG rose 3.4% in the same session, MAR fell 1.6%, and the S&P 500 added 0.6%. Travel demand is a shared input, so industry-wide news about it would have moved these names together. They did not, which puts most of the explanation inside Airbnb.

Nights and seats booked grew 10% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, while gross booking value grew 16%. The gap is a 5% rise in average daily rate, 4% excluding currency, which management says is not just rising prices but a durable reflection of bedroom nights: guests keep booking larger multi-bedroom homes for families and groups, and bedroom nights are running higher and accelerating faster than nights booked. Airbnb is earning more per stay because the stays are getting bigger.

Conversion is doing the rest. In the same quarter, nights booked on the app grew 23% year over year and now make up 64% of the total, and Reserve Now, Pay Later carried over 20% of gross booking value. Hotels are a single-digit share of nights booked but growing about three times as fast as homes, and roughly 35% of first-time hotel guests come back to book a home, so a newer business is feeding the oldest one.

Airbnb’s own AI assistant now settles nearly 45% of the issues it receives without a human agent, and customer support cost per booking fell about 16% year over year in the quarter. That is how adjusted EBITDA margin widened by more than 100 basis points while the company absorbed a material increase in AI spending. Even with that spending, Airbnb produced $4.8 billion of free cash flow over the trailing twelve months on $13.2 billion of revenue. Cash generation of that kind is one of the things the Trefis High Quality Portfolio insists on in its holdings.

sum: Airbnb's second quarter gave investors the clean beat they wanted, but the more interesting signal is where the company is pushing next: hotels, payments, AI - and everything else that happens on a trip.

Airbnb isn't just defending the home-rental business it built. It reported second-quarter 2026 revenue of $3.61 billion on August 6, up 17% from a year earlier, and investors treated the numbers as proof that the company still has room to grow beyond spare rooms and family houses.

The quarter was strong on the basic measures. Analysts had expected $3.58 billion in revenue, according to Zacks Investment Research. Airbnb beat that. Earnings per share came in at $1.37, above the $1.19 estimate Zacks had published before the report. Gross booking value rose 16% to $27.2 billion, while nights and seats booked increased 10% to 148.3 million. Barron's reported that the stock jumped 16% to $175.90 on Friday after the results, its best one-day gain since the company went public.

That kind of move doesn't happen because investors like a tidy earnings table. Money moved because the outlook moved with it. The Wall Street Journal reported that Airbnb raised its full-year revenue growth forecast to at least a mid-teens rate, up from its prior low-to-mid-teens view. For the third quarter, the company projected revenue of $4.69 billion to $4.77 billion, and Barron's noted that Airbnb now expects an adjusted EBITDA margin of at least 35.5% for the year.

Here's how the company did compared with LSEG's consensus of analyst estimates:
Revenue climbed 17% from $3.1 billion a year earlier, Airbnb said in a statement. Net income increased to $816 million from $642 million, or $1.03 per share, a year ago.

For the current period, Airbnb said it expects revenue of between $4.69 billion and $4.77 billion, while analysts had been projecting sales of $4.61 billion, according to LSEG. At the midpoint of the range, year-over-year revenue growth would be about 14%.

Airbnb said that in the U.S. and Canada region and in the area that includes Europe and the Middle East, bookings growth was in the high single digits. For Asia-Pacific, growth was in the high teens, while the Latin America business saw bookings growth of about 20%.

The company highlighted particular strength in Brazil and Mexico, but said, "Overall, we continue to observe market share gains broadly across Latin America, demonstrating the success of our expansion strategy within this region."
Free cash flow jumped 30% to $1.25 billion from $962 million a year earlier, Airbnb said.

Here are three reasons why this travel stock is a smart buy right now.

With 5.5 million hosts listing 9 million properties worldwide and 2.5 billion all-time guest arrivals, Airbnb has built a massive two-sided network effect. This setup makes the business incredibly difficult to disrupt. And the platform is positioned to boost its value proposition over time, as the number of hosts/listings and bookings increases.

Airbnb's brand has also become a key contributor to its success. The company name is so widely recognized that it's used interchangeably as a verb. This is a clear indicator of the mindshare Airbnb has among travelers and hosts.
